cutoff: Earlier effective dates, then same-date case-name alphabetical order before NAHB
method: Fresh source opinion topology review; prior assignment tallies not used as counts. Classification excludes procedural/threshold, summary, per-curiam and source events; Aktepe is uncounted notwithstanding its filename. Each multipart lead contributes once per author.
recommendation: Souter for fit; final selection remains with assembly.
recommendation_basis: The frozen Path A position identifies economic conversion as the very harm-producing activity. Souter can coordinate that application with Sweet Home actual injury and ordinary causation, using Hinds and Robinson to distinguish actual function from surrounding purchases. The opinion must preserve the enacted taking category, reject speculation and unsupported regime grounds, and reserve noneconomic applications. Stevens is the strongest alternative because Hinds performs the property-function distinction. Stone fully joins Path A, but his separate proposed framework supplies no necessary accommodation to the complete shared ground; Breyer is equally eligible at eleven but offers no established advantage over the lower-count candidates. No change to a frozen Associate commitment is proposed.
scope: No Git command used. No preexisting Record, assignment, freeze, or projection modified. The new earlier-effective Record enters future counts and reopens no completed assignment.

On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces under 28 U.S.C. §1259, reviewing 44 M.J. 442. The question is whether Military Rule of Evidence 707's categorical exclusion of polygraph evidence violates the accused's constitutional right to present a defense.

An Air Force investigator administered the examination before the urinalysis result was known. The examiner considered Scheffer's answers to show no deception. At his court-martial, Scheffer denied knowing drug ingestion and sought the examiner's testimony to support his credibility after impeachment. The judge excluded it under Rule 707 without an individualized reliability hearing. The military appellate court removed that categorical obstacle on constitutional grounds; it did not hold this proffer necessarily admissible.

United States v. Hinds; Fourth Circuit No. 97-4030, district case CR-96-148. Plenary merits decision, April 6, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 6. On review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the Fourth Circuit's unpublished October 15, 1997 judgment affirming the §844(i) conviction. The questions are whether the Pleasant Ridge United Church of Christ building was used in interstate commerce or an activity affecting commerce under that statute and, if the statute reaches it, whether that application lies within Congress's Commerce Clause authority. Hinds also presented an Establishment Clause objection below. No separate Supreme Court docket or argument date is established.

Hinds and an accomplice burned the church in Greensboro, North Carolina. Hinds waived a jury and stipulated the elements other than the commerce connection. After hearing evidence on that issue, the District Court denied his motion to dismiss and found him guilty. The Fourth Circuit recited the property-use element, held the evidence sufficient, and rejected the religious objection. The church sent annual funds through its national denomination, employed one full-time and two part-time workers, provided the full-time employee insurance procured from out-of-state companies, and purchased utilities, insurance, religious materials and other goods and services.

A-738 seeks a stay or affirmative injunction pending review of the Fourth Circuit's January 22, 1998 civil judgment, 134 F.3d 622. Paraguay, its Ambassador and Consul General assert their own Vienna Convention and 1859 Friendship Treaty rights; the Consul General also pleaded §1983. The lower court affirmed on immunity grounds, treating the notice violation as completed and the requested relief as retrospective. It did not decide the alternative Rooker-Feldman or political-question defenses. The Fourth Circuit application is presented to Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and by him referred to the Court under its standing practice.

A-767 accompanies an original habeas petition under §§2241 and 2254. It asks for a stay pending disposition of that petition. Time for ICJ consideration and this Court's consideration of the United States' response are the stated purposes, not an automatic extension through the international merits proceeding. The applicant offers certiorari-stay and preliminary-injunction tests expressly as analogies. A-771 accompanies the April 13 motion for leave to file an original complaint invoking Article III and §1251(b)(1); it seeks a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction on the asserted newly threatened breach of the April 9 ICJ measure, Charter obligations, comity and the Consul General's official-capacity §1983 claim. Both original requests are before the Court as original filings; neither is recited as a circuit referral.

The ICJ proceeding began April 3. Its April 9 provisional measure asks the United States to take all measures at its disposal to prevent execution pending its final decision and to inform the ICJ of measures taken. Its preliminary jurisdiction and urgency determinations reserve the treaty remedy and the relevance of prejudice. The present questions concern immediate domestic protection through three distinct channels. A-732 is not decided in this order; neither certiorari petition, the original habeas petition nor the original-action leave motion receives a final disposition.

Women’s Medical Professional Corp. v. Voinovich; Sixth Circuit Nos. 96-3157 and 96-3159. Plenary merits decision, April 20, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 7. On review of the Sixth Circuit’s final judgment, 130 F.3d 187, entered November 18, 1997. No argument date or separate Supreme Court docket is supplied.

The questions are whether Casey’s abortion-review standard or Salerno’s no-valid-applications formulation governs this facial challenge; whether Ohio’s D&X prohibition fails because of its definition, clinical reach, notice or criminal and civil culpability provisions; and whether postviability law must permit necessary abortion to avert severe, lasting and potentially irreversible mental or emotional injury. The Court addresses the complete Casey standard rather than adopting an independent numerical facial threshold.

Ohio’s H.B.135 created an all-stage method prohibition, a separate postviability prohibition, viability-testing requirements and related clinical duties. The district court’s preliminary injunction became permanent on January 12, 1996 after consolidation with trial by stipulation. The Sixth Circuit sustained an injunction against the whole Act, relying on the method definition’s overlap with D&E, clinical-fault concerns, serious mental-health exclusion and inseverability. Those legal conclusions remain subject to review. The lower standing ruling and the State’s failure to contest it in the court of appeals supply no new standing holding here.

Under §2919.17(A), purposeful performance, inducement or attempted performance or inducement of an abortion on a viable fetus is prohibited unless a physician, acting in good faith and using reasonable medical judgment, determines either that abortion is necessary to prevent maternal death or a serious risk of substantial and irreversible impairment of a major bodily function, or that the fetus is not viable after the assessment required by §2919.18(A). The latter provision requires, beginning with the twenty-second week, a good-faith determination of nonviability using reasonable medical judgment, after examining the patient and performing or arranging the viability tests a reasonable physician would use. Its medical-emergency exception excuses that testing obligation. The separate twenty-four-week viability presumption is rebuttable.

Section 2919.16(F) defines the emergency through the physician’s good-faith, reasonable medical assessment of a pregnancy complication: immediate abortion must be needed to prevent the patient’s death or to avoid a serious risk, created by delay, of substantial and irreversible impairment of a major bodily function. Section 2919.16(J) separately defines that serious-risk category by a medically diagnosed condition complicating the pregnancy that directly or indirectly causes such impairment. Its nonexclusive examples are preeclampsia, inevitable abortion, prematurely ruptured membranes, diabetes and multiple sclerosis. These enacted categories remain distinct from the constitutional protection and the method-prohibition defenses addressed below.

records.event:
Miller v. Albright, No. 96-1060. Plenary merits decision, April 22, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 7. Argued November 4, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the D.C. Circuit. The question concerns unequal citizenship-transmission requirements for a child born abroad to a citizen father rather than a citizen mother.

Miller was born in the Philippines on June 20, 1970. Her November 1991 citizenship application was denied; she applied again after a July 1992 Texas decree established the biological and legal parent-child relationship with her citizen father. The State Department accepted his citizenship and sufficient physical presence to transmit citizenship. Paternity is undisputed, although no formal clear-and-convincing finding is reported. The denial expressly rested on §1409(a)(4). The father initially sued with her, was dismissed, did not appeal, and the action was transferred from Texas to the District of Columbia. The district court dismissed for lack of power to grant the requested citizenship; the court of appeals recognized standing but sustained the statutory distinction.

The amended §1409(a) separately requires clear-and-convincing proof of blood relationship; the father's United States nationality at birth; his written agreement, unless deceased, to support the person until eighteen; and, while the person is under eighteen, legitimation under residence or domicile law, his written sworn acknowledgment, or competent-court paternity adjudication. The last alternatives are disjunctive. Miller may elect the former subsection, which required legitimation before twenty-one and did not contain the later support promise. Her decree followed both age deadlines. The former route retains the separate §1401 transmission predicates; the earlier ten-year presence period, including five years after fourteen, differs from the amended five-year period, including two after fourteen. The agency accepted sufficient presence; no deficiency under either applicable version is found.

Section 1409(c) separately gives the citizen mother's nationality at birth to a person born abroad and out of wedlock after December 23, 1952 when the mother previously had continuous physical presence for one year in the United States or an outlying possession. The constitutionality of the differing presence periods and every independent support application are outside this decision. No amended support or blood-proof requirement is added to the former-law route.

Moore offered Geissal COBRA continuation after terminating his employment. He elected it; six months later Moore renounced it because he already had coverage through his wife's employer's group plan when he elected. His wife substituted after his death. Hopkins v. Reeves, No. 96-1693. Plenary merits decision, June 8, 1998. Argued February 23, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.

Reeves was convicted of two Nebraska felony murders arising from sexual assault or attempted sexual assault. The trial court refused instructions on second-degree murder and manslaughter because Nebraska does not classify them as lesser included offenses of felony murder. A three-judge panel later imposed death. The Eighth Circuit rejected a separate due-process ground but granted conditional habeas relief on the instruction theory. The question is whether Beck requires these nonincluded alternatives in a capital prosecution.

Muscarello v. United States, No. 96-1654, and Cleveland et al. v. United States, No. 96-8837. Consolidated plenary merits decision, June 8, 1998. Both argued March 23, 1998. On writs of certiorari to the Fifth and First Circuits, respectively.

Muscarello transported marijuana for sale in a truck with a handgun locked in its glove compartment. The Cleveland matter concerns guns in a car trunk accompanying the drug transaction.
